oneLine: God's loyal love works through ordinary faithfulness, all the way to Jesus.
intro: A short story in four chapters about a grieving widow, a loyal foreigner and a kind farmer, set in and around Bethlehem. God hardly 'does' anything dramatic in it, yet he is quietly at work on every page, and the last verse points straight to Christmas.

context.p: 'In the days when the judges ruled', around 1100 BC: a chaotic, violent time in Israel when 'everyone did as they saw fit' (Judges 21:25). Ruth is a quiet light in a dark time.
Bethlehem (its name means 'house of bread') and Moab, a neighbouring country across the Dead Sea that was often Israel's enemy.
Naomi, an Israelite widow who loses everything; Ruth, her Moabite daughter-in-law who refuses to leave her; and Boaz, a respected farmer and relative of Naomi's late husband.

The story ends with Ruth's great-grandson, King David. Centuries later, David's descendant Jesus was born in the same town, and Matthew lists Ruth in Jesus's family tree (Matthew 1:5). Boaz the 'redeemer' is a picture of Jesus.

threads: God at work behind the scenes

weeks.title: Where you go, I will go
weeks.big: What does it look like to stick with someone when life falls apart?
context: A famine drives Elimelech, Naomi and their two sons from Bethlehem to Moab. Moabites were not allowed to join God's people (Deuteronomy 23:3), but the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then all three men die.

A widow in that world had no income, no protection and no future unless a man in the family provided for her. Naomi is old, far from home, with nothing. She tells her daughters-in-law to go back to their families. Orpah goes. Ruth refuses.
The big Hebrew word in Ruth is hesed: loyal, committed, more-than-you-have-to love. It's the word the Bible uses for God's love for his people. Watch for it all through the book.
Notice the last line of the chapter: they arrive 'as the barley harvest was beginning'. The writer is dropping a hint that the story isn't over.
words: Leaders God raised up before Israel had kings.
A long time without enough food.
A neighbouring country, often Israel's enemy.
Loyal, committed love that goes beyond duty. The word is translated 'kindness' in 1:8.
notice: Why do Naomi and her family leave Bethlehem?
What does Orpah do? What does Ruth do?
What does Naomi ask to be called when she gets home, and why?

dig.q: Ruth had every reason to go home. Why do you think she stayed?
dig.a: Staying meant leaving her country, family and gods for a poor, grieving old woman, among people who looked down on Moabites. She stayed out of loyal love, and because she had come to trust Naomi's God: 'your God my God'.

dig.q: Naomi says 'the LORD has afflicted me' and calls herself 'bitter'. Was she wrong to say it?
dig.a: She's honest about her grief, and the Bible doesn't hide it. But she can't see the whole story yet. As she speaks, she's standing next to Ruth, God's gift to her, at the start of the harvest.

dig.q: What's the difference between loyalty when it's easy and loyalty when it costs something?
dig.a: Anyone can stick around when things are fun. Hesed shows up when someone is grieving, difficult or has nothing to give back. That's how God loves us.

dig.q: God doesn't do anything dramatic in this chapter. Where is he?
dig.a: Quietly at work: ending the famine, bringing Ruth, timing the harvest. Ruth teaches us to trust that God is at work even when we can't see him.

weeks.young: Who is someone who stuck with you when you were sad or in trouble? How did it feel?
weeks.principle: Loyal love sticks with people when it's hard, and God is at work even when life feels bitter.
weeks.why: Families are where loyalty gets tested: when someone is grumpy, grieving or difficult. Ruth shows what love that stays looks like.

jesus.text: And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.
jesus.note: Jesus promised the same loyal love: he will never leave.

also.text: And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose.
also.note: God is at work even in Naomi's worst years.

scenarios: A friend is going through a hard time and isn't much fun to be around.
Someone in the family is grumpy or sad.
A friend is being left out by everyone else.
tryThis: Each person picks someone having a hard time and sticks with them this week: sit with them, message them, include them.
When someone in the family is upset, stay with them instead of walking away.
Make 'hesed' the family word of the month: spot it and name it when you see it.
weeks.pray: Pray for someone you know who is grieving or lonely. Ask God to help you be loyal like Ruth.

anchor.text: But Ruth replied, 'Don't urge me to leave you or to turn back from you. Where you go I will go, and where you stay I will stay. Your people will be my people and your God my God.'

stretch.text: Where you die I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if even death separates you and me.

weeks.title: Under his wings
weeks.big: How does God look after people who have nothing?
context: God's law told farmers not to harvest the edges of their fields or go back for what they dropped. The leftovers were for the poor, the foreigner and the widow to gather: 'gleaning' (Leviticus 19:9–10). Ruth was all three.

Gleaning was hard and risky: a foreign woman alone in the fields could be mistreated. Boaz tells his men not to touch her, lets her drink from their water jars and eat with his workers, and quietly has them drop extra barley for her.
Ruth 'happened' to end up in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi's husband. The writer is smiling as he says it: in Ruth, there are no accidents.

'Under whose wings' pictures a mother bird sheltering her chicks. Ruth has come to shelter under the God of Israel. An ephah of barley (verse 17) was about 13 kilograms: weeks of food from one day's work.
words: Gathering what the harvesters left behind.
A grain used to make bread.
A close relative responsible for rescuing family members in trouble.
notice: How does Boaz greet his workers?
What does Boaz do for Ruth? List everything.
Why is Naomi so excited when she hears whose field it was?

dig.q: Ruth 'happened' to work in Boaz's field. Was it chance?
dig.a: The writer wants us to see God's hand. God guides ordinary choices: which field, which day. Looking back, we often see his care in what felt like coincidence.

dig.q: Boaz goes far beyond what the law required. What does that show about him?
dig.a: The law said leave the edges. Boaz protects Ruth, feeds her and has extra dropped for her, without making her feel like a charity case. Generosity that protects people's dignity is hesed too.

dig.q: Boaz had heard all about Ruth before he met her. What had he heard, and why does it matter?
dig.a: That she had left everything to look after Naomi. Character gets noticed. Ruth's quiet loyalty at home was talked about in town.

dig.q: Boaz prays that God will reward Ruth, then becomes the answer to his own prayer. What can we learn from that?
dig.a: Sometimes when we pray for someone, God says: you go. Kindness is often how God answers prayer.

weeks.young: Have you seen a mother bird with her chicks under her wings? Why do the chicks hide there?
weeks.principle: God cares for outsiders and people in need, often through ordinary people's kindness, so be someone's Boaz.
weeks.why: It's easy to notice people like us. Boaz noticed a poor foreign widow and treated her with honour. That's how God treats us.

jesus.text: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing.
jesus.note: Jesus used the same picture of wings for how he longs to protect his people.

also.text: When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. Do not go over your vineyard a second time or pick up the grapes that have fallen. Leave them for the poor and the foreigner. I am the LORD your God.
He will cover you with his feathers, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness will be your shield and rampart.

scenarios: A new family arrives at school or church from another country.
Someone has less than you: lunch, clothes, money.
You could do the minimum to help, or a bit more.
tryThis: Leave the edges: give away something you could have kept (pocket money, a toy, food for the food bank).
Do one generous thing that goes beyond what was asked.
Welcome someone new: invite them, sit with them, learn their name.
weeks.pray: Thank God for how he has looked after your family. Pray for refugees and people far from home this Christmas.

anchor.text: May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge.

weeks.title: A woman of noble character
weeks.big: What do people see in you when no one is telling you what to do?
context: The harvest is over and Naomi wants a secure future for Ruth. She knows Boaz is a 'guardian-redeemer': a close relative who could marry Ruth, protect her, and keep the family's land and name alive.

The threshing floor was where grain was separated from husks, and workers slept there to guard the harvest. Ruth's request, 'spread the corner of your garment over me', was a respectful way of asking Boaz to marry her and take her under his protection. It uses the same Hebrew word as the 'wings' Boaz prayed about in chapter 2.
Boaz praises Ruth's 'kindness' (hesed again) and promises to do things properly, in public, even though another relative has the first right to marry her.
'Noble character' is the same phrase used for the wife in Proverbs 31. In the Hebrew Bible, Ruth comes straight after Proverbs, as if to say: here's a real one.
words: A close relative with the duty to rescue family members.
Where grain was beaten to separate it from the husks.
Tossing grain in the wind so the light husks blow away.
Strong, good and worthy of respect.
notice: What does Naomi tell Ruth to do?
Why can't Boaz just say yes straight away?

dig.q: Ruth was brave. What was risky about what she did?
dig.a: She was a poor foreigner asking a rich, important man to marry her. He could have refused or shamed her. She trusted Naomi, trusted Boaz's character, and trusted God.

dig.q: Boaz could have taken a short cut. Why does he insist on doing things the right way?
dig.a: Integrity means doing what's right even when no one would know. There was a closer relative, and Boaz respected that, even though he might lose Ruth. He trusted God with the outcome.

dig.q: Everyone in town knew Ruth was a woman of 'noble character'. How do people get a reputation like that?
dig.a: Not in one big moment, but in thousands of small faithful ones: caring for Naomi, working hard, being kind. Character is what you do over and over.

dig.q: Ruth asks for Boaz's 'garment' over her; Boaz had prayed for God's 'wings' over her. How do they connect?
dig.a: Boaz becomes the way God answers. God's protection reaches Ruth through a faithful man. That's often how God works: through his people.

weeks.young: If nobody was watching you today, would you behave the same? Why does that matter?
weeks.principle: Character is built in small faithful choices, so be brave, be kind and do things God's way.
weeks.why: We're all tempted by short cuts. Ruth and Boaz show that doing it the right way, and waiting, is worth it.

jesus.text: Do to others as you would have them do to you.
jesus.note: Jesus's golden rule: Boaz and Ruth both lived it.

also.text: A good name is more desirable than great riches; to be esteemed is better than silver or gold.
also.note: A good reputation is worth more than money.

also.text: Charm is deceptive, and beauty is fleeting; but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.

scenarios: You could cheat in a test or game and no one would know.
You need to ask for something important and you're nervous.
Doing something properly will take longer than a short cut.
tryThis: Each person names one quality they'd like to be known for, and does one thing a day that builds it.
No short cuts this week: do jobs and homework properly, even when no one checks.
At dinner, say something specific you admire about each person's character.
weeks.pray: Ask God to build noble character in each of you, and for courage to do one brave, right thing this week.

anchor.text: And now, my daughter, don't be afraid. I will do for you all you ask. All the people of my town know that you are a woman of noble character.

weeks.title: The redeemer
weeks.big: What does it cost to rescue someone?
context: The town gate was where business and legal matters were settled in front of the elders. Boaz sits there and waits for the closer relative.

The relative wants Naomi's land, until he hears that marrying Ruth comes with it. Any son would carry on Elimelech's family name and inherit the land, so the relative would pay and gain nothing. He backs out. Boaz pays the cost gladly. Taking off a sandal sealed the deal, like signing a contract.
Ruth and Boaz have a son, Obed. Naomi, once empty and bitter, holds a grandson in her arms.

Then the last verses zoom out: Obed is the grandfather of King David. Matthew's list of Jesus's ancestors includes Boaz and Ruth the Moabite (Matthew 1:5). A foreign widow's loyalty became part of the family line of the Saviour, born centuries later in the same town: Bethlehem.
words: The 'town hall' of an ancient city.
Buy back; rescue at a cost.
Land or property passed down in a family.
notice: Why does the other relative change his mind?
What do the women say to Naomi?

dig.q: The other relative said no because it would cost him. Boaz said yes even though it cost him. What does that tell us?
dig.a: Rescuing someone always costs something. Boaz paid to rescue a family when someone else had the first duty. Love that rescues is costly love.

dig.q: How is Boaz a picture of Jesus?
dig.a: Jesus is our guardian-redeemer: our relative (he became human), able to pay, and willing to pay at great cost, his own life. He brings outsiders like Ruth, and like us, into his family.

dig.q: Compare Naomi at the start of the book and at the end. What's changed?
dig.a: She went from 'full' to 'empty' and 'bitter'. Now she's full again: family, food and a future. God hadn't forgotten her when she felt forgotten.

dig.q: Why do you think God put a Moabite woman in Jesus's family tree?
dig.a: To show from the start that God's family is for every nation. Being an outsider doesn't keep anyone out of God's story.

weeks.young: Ruth lived in Bethlehem. Who else was born in Bethlehem many years later?
weeks.principle: God weaves ordinary faithfulness into his big story, which leads to Jesus, our Redeemer.
weeks.why: Ruth never knew she'd be King David's great-grandmother or part of Jesus's family. Our small faithful choices matter more than we can see.

jesus.text: For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
jesus.note: Jesus paid the price to rescue us, like Boaz but far more.

also.text: Salmon the father of Boaz, whose mother was Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed, whose mother was Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse,
But when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship.

scenarios: Helping someone will cost you time, money or something you wanted.
You feel your small acts of kindness make no difference.
Someone you know will have a hard or lonely Christmas.
tryThis: Do one costly kindness as a family this Christmas: invite someone who'll be alone, give generously, or serve somewhere.
Read Matthew 1:1–17 and find Ruth (and the other surprising names).
Each person tells one way they've seen God at work this month, like Naomi looking back.
weeks.pray: Thank Jesus for being our Redeemer, who paid the price to bring us into his family.

anchor.text: The women said to Naomi: 'Praise be to the LORD, who this day has not left you without a guardian-redeemer. May he become famous throughout Israel!'

stretch.text: And they named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.

checkin: Say this week's verse together from memory. Who can say it alone?
How did our 'This week we will' go? Where did we actually see it happen?
What is one thing from this passage you want to keep doing?
Read the Principles wall aloud: every principle so far this month.
